title: Finding Causes Across Sites and Years
endLine: Follow populations for years, compare sites, and test every rival cause.

scenes.tts: How do you find a cause in nature without a lab? You often cannot randomly assign drought, competitors, or warming to wild populations. Yet nature imposes events of its own. Following populations across years and sites turns those events into tests.
scenes.caption: How do you find a cause in nature without a lab? You often cannot randomly assign drought, competitors, or warming to wild populations. Yet nature imposes events of its own. Following populations across years and sites turns those events into tests.
scenes.visual: Establish the carried world filling the frame: a wide landscape of three wild sites (a focal valley and comparison sites) with gently drifting bird silhouettes above and a multi-year timeline bar along the bottom (all schematic). A question banner appears first ('Cause without a lab?') as a faded lab glassware outline dissolves away. As drought cracks, an arriving competitor silhouette, and a rising warmth shimmer sweep the focal site, the bottom timeline lights up and markers drop onto the sites.
scenes.narration: How do you find a cause in nature without a lab? You often cannot randomly assign drought, competitors, or warming to wild populations. Yet nature imposes events of its own. Following populations across years and sites turns those events into tests.

scenes.tts: In a natural experiment, nature supplies an event without random assignment. In a long-term study, you measure the same population every year. Returning matters: one year's weather can dominate a snapshot.
scenes.caption: In a natural experiment, nature supplies an event without random assignment. In a long-term study, you measure the same population every year. Returning matters: one year's weather can dominate a snapshot.
scenes.visual: Carry the same landscape and bottom timeline. First, a disturbance wave sweeps the focal site with a bold label ('Natural experiment') and a crossed-out random-assignment icon. Then the timeline marker steps smoothly year by year ('Long-term study') as a schematic trend line builds above the focal site; a sharp single-year weather spike flashes on one year and fades against the steadier multi-year curve.
scenes.narration: In a natural experiment, nature supplies an event without random assignment. In a long-term study, you measure the same population every year. Returning matters: one year's weather can dominate a snapshot.

scenes.tts: Comparing sites in one year helps, yet space is not time. Young blue chromis, a reef fish, showed a crowding effect across reefs: a pattern in space. Showing numbers return to a level needs records through time. Long records also catch time lags, as when winter food limits next spring's births.
scenes.caption: Comparing sites in one year helps, yet space is not time. Young blue chromis, a reef fish, showed a crowding effect across reefs: a pattern in space. scenes.visual: Transform the carried sites into reef patches side by side while the bottom timeline locks onto one year ('One year: space'). Schematic schools of young blue chromis swim across the reefs at differing densities, tracing an across-site crowding slope (schematic, labelled 'Pattern in space'). Then unlock the timeline across seasons: a schematic winter food bar dips first, and after a clear delay the next spring's birth pulse dips, showing why long records are needed.

scenes.tts: Without random assignment, you test causes by tracking years, comparing sites, and ruling out rivals. Mismatch is a gap between the prey peak and laying dates. Both and colleagues compared Dutch pied flycatcher populations whose prey peaks differed in timing. If mismatch matters, decline should be steepest where the gap is largest.
scenes.caption: Without random assignment, you test causes by tracking years, comparing sites, and ruling out rivals. Mismatch is a gap between the prey peak and laying dates. Both and colleagues compared Dutch pied flycatcher populations whose prey peaks differed in timing. If mismatch matters, decline should be steepest where the gap is largest.
scenes.visual: Return the carried landscape to multiple woodland breeding sites over the advancing multi-year timeline (schematic). Three high-contrast tags light up in turn ('Track years', 'Compare sites', 'Rule out rivals'). Above the woodlands, Dutch pied flycatcher silhouettes appear beside schematic prey-peak curves shifted to different dates at each site. Below each site, paired schematic vital-rate bars ('Births' and 'Survival') rise and fall as the timeline advances.
scenes.narration: Without random assignment, you test causes by tracking years, comparing sites, and ruling out rivals. Mismatch is a gap between the prey peak and laying dates. Both and colleagues compared Dutch pied flycatcher populations whose prey peaks differed in timing. If mismatch matters, decline should be steepest where the gap is largest.

scenes.tts: Suppose flycatchers decline where mismatch is large. Each year you track breeding success, survival of young, and wintering adult survival. If falling wintering adult survival explains most of the decline, is mismatch likely the main cause?
scenes.caption: Suppose flycatchers decline where mismatch is large. Each year you track breeding success, survival of young, and wintering adult survival. If falling wintering adult survival explains most of the decline, is mismatch likely the main cause?
scenes.visual: Zoom within the carried woodland world onto a site where the schematic prey-peak curve pulls ahead of the egg-laying marker while population numbers slope down. Split the vital-rate display into two moving schematic tracks: 'Breeding and young' over the breeding site on the left, and 'Wintering adults' over a connected wintering ground on the right. As the wintering adult survival track drops steeply, the question settles at top: 'Wintering adults drop: is mismatch the main cause?'
scenes.narration: Suppose flycatchers decline where mismatch is large. Each year you track breeding success, survival of young, and wintering adult survival. If falling wintering adult survival explains most of the decline, is mismatch likely the main cause?

scenes.visual: Hold the carried breeding-and-wintering split world and the top question ('Wintering adults drop: is mismatch the main cause?') on screen for a deliberate thinking pause, with a gentle ambient pulse on the two schematic vital-rate tracks and a quiet progress arc; no new labels enter.

scenes.tts: Unlikely. Mismatch should show up mainly in breeding success and survival of young. Carry-over effects, where one season affects the next, can blur that line. So test habitat, predators and disease, and try feeding birds after the prey peak.
scenes.caption: Unlikely. Mismatch should show up mainly in breeding success and survival of young. Carry-over effects, where one season affects the next, can blur that line. So test habitat, predators and disease, and try feeding birds after the prey peak.
scenes.visual: Resolve the carried split world: highlight the 'Breeding and young' track as where mismatch should appear, dimming the mismatch arrow when 'Wintering adults' drives the decline. Draw a glowing seasonal bridge from one season to the next ('Carry-over effect') that slightly blurs the boundary between tracks. Along the breeding site and migration route, three rival-check markers light up ('Habitat', 'Predators', 'Disease'), and a supplementary feeding station appears at one site after the prey peak, tagged 'Test: does food timing limit breeding?'.
scenes.narration: Unlikely. Mismatch should show up mainly in breeding success and survival of young. Carry-over effects, where one season affects the next, can blur that line. So test habitat, predators and disease, and try feeding birds after the prey peak.

scenes.tts: Still, wild comparisons can mislead. Two sites differ in soils, species pools, and history, confounders that mimic a cause. A statistical model exposes a rival driver it measured, not one it missed. Detection shows change beyond chance; attribution tests its cause.
scenes.caption: Still, wild comparisons can mislead. Two sites differ in soils, species pools, and history, confounders that mimic a cause. A statistical model exposes a rival driver it measured, not one it missed. Detection shows change beyond chance; attribution tests its cause.
scenes.visual: Keep two carried landscape sites side by side and peel back the ground beneath them to show distinct soil layers, species silhouettes, and disturbance scars ('Confounders'). Overlay a clean schematic model frame that illuminates a measured rival-driver bar while a darkened unmeasured bar stays hidden behind the terrain. On the bottom timeline, a rising line clears a pale chance band ('Detection') before branching into competing driver tests ('Attribution').
scenes.narration: Still, wild comparisons can mislead. Two sites differ in soils, species pools, and history, confounders that mimic a cause. A statistical model exposes a rival driver it measured, not one it missed. Detection shows change beyond chance; attribution tests its cause.

scenes.tts: On Daphne Major in the Galapagos, Peter and Rosemary Grant tracked medium ground finches. Twenty-two years after the large ground finch arrived, the two species together severely depleted the food. Their beak sizes then diverged. Yet a coinciding drought stayed hard to rule out.
scenes.caption: On Daphne Major in the Galapagos, Peter and Rosemary Grant tracked medium ground finches. 22 years after the large ground finch arrived, the two species together severely depleted the food. Their beak sizes then diverged. Yet a coinciding drought stayed hard to rule out.
scenes.visual: Morph the carried focal site into an island silhouette ('Daphne Major, Galapagos') over the bottom timeline spanning 22 years (schematic). Medium ground finch silhouettes forage on the island; a large ground finch silhouette arrives at the start. As the timeline reaches 22 years, seed icons thin out sharply as both finch species feed (food depleted) while the schematic beak-size track for medium ground finches diverges away from the large finch; a drought cloud overlaps the same interval with a caution tag ('Competition vs. drought').
scenes.narration: On Daphne Major in the Galapagos, Peter and Rosemary Grant tracked medium ground finches. 22 years after the large ground finch arrived, the two species together severely depleted the food. Their beak sizes then diverged. Yet a coinciding drought stayed hard to rule out.

scenes.tts: Comparisons also test migration load, a fitness drop from immigrant genes suited elsewhere. Timema walking-sticks live on two host plants, with colour morphs camouflaged differently on each. In 2007, Daniel Bolnick and Patrik Nosil compared twenty-five populations. Those receiving more immigrants were more poorly matched, and selection shifted their morphs more. It is a correlation, not a manipulation.
scenes.caption: Comparisons also test migration load, a fitness drop from immigrant genes suited elsewhere. Timema walking-sticks live on two host plants, with colour morphs camouflaged differently on each. In 2007, Daniel Bolnick and Patrik Nosil compared 25 populations. Those receiving more immigrants were more poorly matched, and selection shifted their morphs more. It is a correlation, not a manipulation.
scenes.visual: Morph the carried multi-site landscape into a schematic array representing 25 natural walking-stick populations across two distinct host-plant colours (Bolnick and Nosil, 2007). Each colour morph blends into one host and stands out on the other (schematic). Curved arrows carry contrasting colour morphs from one host plant into the other, heavier into some sites than others. Above sites with heavier immigration, a schematic mismatch gauge widens and selection-shift arrows grow bolder; a bottom tag appears ('Correlation, not manipulation').
scenes.narration: Comparisons also test migration load, a fitness drop from immigrant genes suited elsewhere. scenes.tts: In 2008, Rosenzweig and colleagues linked continental-scale warming to observed biological and physical shifts. Natural climate variation alone could not explain those changes. Still, data clustered in Europe and North America, a biased sample. Track years and sites, test rivals, and nature's records can reveal causes.

scenes.visual: Pull the carried sites outward into a schematic continental map (Rosenzweig and colleagues, 2008) where a warm tint spreads and schematic shift markers climb above a pale natural-variation band. Highlight where data cluster densely across Europe and North America and stay sparse elsewhere ('Biased global sample'). Then settle smoothly back into the carried sites, advancing timeline, and rival-check brackets moving in sync.
